g.text: Yernur Kenzhegazin · Alan Berdigaliyev · Hugo Telles
M2 GENIOMHE-AI | Supervisor: Amaury Giard, IBISC

text.style: font-weight: 600; font-size: 28px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #22272d

g.text: Chemical compounds can change a cell’s gene expression.
Predicting this response could help prioritize experiments.
However, low error may reflect the control state rather than
a learned chemical effect, making simple baselines essential [2].

text.style: font-weight: 600; font-size: 28px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #22272d

g.text: Does chemical structure add predictive value?
We use LINCS L1000 bulk expression data to predict 978 genes
from chemical structure and matched control measurements.
Three multilayer perceptrons (MLPs), retrained PRnet [1] and
baselines are tested on new compounds, SKBR3 and GEO studies.

text.style: font-weight: 600; font-size: 26px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #ffffff
font-weight: 600; font-size: 26px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #ffffff
font-weight: 600; font-size: 26px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #ffffff

g.text: Seven GEO studies · six gene directions per study
MSE measures expression-prediction error: lower is better.
The linear baseline leads (0.635); all chemical MLPs have
lower error than PRnet, but do not outperform this baseline.
SKBR3 was excluded from training. Adding the training
mean response to measured controls gives the lowest
error (0.551), below every neural network in this test.
Each cell shows correct up/down predictions out of six,
averaged over three seeds; darker means more correct.
These studies show no clear advantage over PRnet.
A–B: circles = seeds; diamond = mean; line = seed range. Dashed: unchanged control.
Only 15 of 42 observed gene directions show clear changes.

text.style: font-weight: 600; font-size: 28px; font-family: 'Inter'; text-anchor: start; fill: #22272d

g.text: Chemical MLPs have lower MSE than PRnet here; simple baselines remain strongest.
Beating PRnet here does not establish added value from chemistry. One held-out cell line, a small external panel and reused tests limit generalization.
[1] Qi et al., Nature Communications (2024), doi:10.1038/s41467-024-53457-1
